correctness.rationale: For every nonzero normal, reconstruct the central section as chords of the horizontal square at each height, derive the explicit inverse-arctangent expression and limits, and prove balancing by the positive secant-kernel integral. Along balanced normals, the exact derivative reduces to T(r), whose integrand is strictly increasing in r² with endpoint signs -4 and 4/3; this proves the sole meridional dip and sharp π√2 upper bound. The inscribed ball gives area≥π; strict radial excess except for x=0,y=0 proves equality. Brunn concavity and strict shifted-diagonal chord comparison extend the upper bound to all affine planes. Checker compares 159 directions against independent polar and chord integrals and symbolically checks a key integral identity. Its floating-point tests do not substitute for global proof.

originality.rationale: The completed primary descriptions and the dated classical bicylinder exposition supply volume, surface area and axial square sections but not the all-orientation planar-section area, strict normal-balancing law, exact equality sets or unique interior dip. A 2019 applied account reports axis-aligned slicing, while the 2025 arXiv manuscript varies intersection depth to study full-body volume and surface area. The plausible earlier Moore 1974 and Angell–Moore 1987 symmetric-cylinder studies could be inspected only through extracts or bibliographic metadata, so historical priority remains provisional and a potential unrecognized stronger theorem is a residual risk. The available comparisons are implications-based, not title-only.

value.rationale: The full directional section-area profile and exact all-affine maximizing orientations give an intrinsic extremal invariant of the well-studied Steinmetz bicylinder, where only axial square and disk sections are standard. Strict balancing and the unique tilted-meridian dip explain geometry across directions rather than merely calculating one special plane. Such an all-orientation benchmark is natural for section inequalities and geometric integration; no artificial tuning or unsupported downstream theorem is required.
